content: The available data on pesticides used for vector control in drinking water is insufficient to derive health-based guideline values. However, these pesticides typically occur in drinking water at concentrations significantly below levels of health concern. Sodium, at levels found in drinking water, does not pose a health concern. Spinosad is not considered appropriate for setting guideline values for pesticides used in vector control in drinking water. Sulfate, at levels found in drinking water, does not pose a health concern. Temephos is not considered appropriate for setting guideline values for pesticides used in vector control in drinking water. Total dissolved solids, at levels found in drinking water, do not pose a health concern. The data available for trichloramine is inadequate to derive health-based guideline values. The data available for trichloroacetonitrile is inadequate to derive health-based guideline values. Trichlorobenzenes (total) occur in drinking water at concentrations well below levels of health concern. Any health-based value derived would exceed the lowest reported odor threshold. 1,1,1-Trichloroethane occurs in drinking water at concentrations well below levels of health concern. Zinc, at levels found in drinking water, does not pose a health concern. Health-based values have been developed for several chemicals, while provisional reference values have been established for anatoxins and silver. These values may guide actions by Member States when there is a reason for local concern. Where health-based values or provisional reference values have been established, this information is detailed in the chemical fact sheets in Chapter 12. For substances that may affect the acceptability of drinking water, such as taste, odor, or appearance, refer to Chapter 10. Dicofol does not meet one of the three criteria for evaluation in the Guidelines. However, a background document has been prepared, and a health-based value has been established in response to a request from Member States for guidance. For polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, refer to the relevant fact sheet. Aminomethylphosphonic acid is a specific compound of interest. (2-Methyl-4-chlorophenoxy)acetic acid is another compound of interest. 3-Chloro-4-dichloromethyl-5-hydroxy-2(5H)-furanone is a compound of interest. Tributyltin, triphenyltin, dibutyltin, and di-n-octyltin are specific organotin compounds of interest. Monomethyltin, dimethyltin, and dimethyltin dichloride are specific organotin compounds of interest. Chlorine residuals should be maintained throughout the distribution system to ensure effective disinfection. For free chlorine, a concentration of 2 mg/L is recommended. For total manganese, a provisional guideline value has been established because the calculated guideline value is below the achievable quantification level. For substances considered carcinogenic, the guideline value represents the concentration in drinking water associated with an upper-bound excess lifetime cancer risk of 1 in 100,000 (10^-5) over 70 years of exposure. Concentrations associated with risks of 1 in 10,000 (10^-4) and 1 in 1,000,000 (10^-6) can be calculated by multiplying or dividing the guideline value by 10, respectively. For bottle-fed infants, refer to the respective chemical fact sheet in Chapter 12 for specific considerations. 2,4-Dichlorophenoxyacetic acid and 2,4-Dichlorophenoxybutyric acid are specific compounds of interest. Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) is a compound of interest. 2,4,5-Trichlorophenoxyacetic acid is another compound of interest. Analytical methods for chemical analysis include volumetric titration, colorimetric methods, UV absorption, atomic absorption spectrometry (AAS), flame atomic absorption spectrometry (FAAS), electrothermal atomic absorption spectrometry (EAAS), inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry (ICP-AES), inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS), chromatography (including gas chromatography and high-performance liquid chromatography), and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Each method has specific applications, advantages, and limitations. For example, FAAS is highly sensitive and free from spectral interference but is not suitable for simultaneous multi-element analysis. EAAS offers higher sensitivity and lower detection limits than FAAS but requires longer analysis times. ICP-AES and ICP-MS allow for multi-element analysis with low detection limits and reduced chemical interference. Chromatography techniques, such as gas chromatography (GC) and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), are used for separating and quantifying organic and inorganic compounds. GC-MS combines gas chromatography with mass spectrometry for enhanced identification and quantification of trace organic compounds. ELISA is a biochemical method used to detect specific chemicals, such as microcystins and synthetic surfactants, by utilizing antibodies and enzyme reactions to produce measurable color changes. For agricultural chemicals and water treatment substances, various analytical methods are applicable, including GC, HPLC, and ICP techniques. Specific methods are chosen based on the chemical properties and required sensitivity.
